items.title: Lesson 2 Focus Question: What are some different ways of describing and representing the motion of a train leaving a station?

answer.html: The motion can be described with words, pictures, a motion diagram (with position and displacement vectors), a data table of position and time, a position-time graph, and an equation, all using a coordinate system with an origin and a positive direction.

check.html: Each representation shows the same train motion in a different form.

items.title: Lesson 2, Infer (Figure 7): A flag is 8 m to the right of the origin on a number line. What position would you give the flag if you chose the direction left of the origin as positive?

body.html: The sign of a position depends on the chosen positive direction. The flag is on the side opposite to the positive direction.

answer.html: −8 m (negative, since left is now the positive direction and the flag is to the right).

check.html: Reversing the positive direction flips the sign but not the magnitude.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: Explain how to decide whether the position of a bird feeder is positive or negative when the origin is placed at the back door of a house.

answer.html: First choose a positive direction (for example, away from the house into the yard). A feeder located in the positive direction from the door has a positive position; one located in the opposite direction (for example, behind the house) has a negative position.

check.html: The sign comes from the direction chosen, not from the object.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: Classify each quantity as a vector or a scalar: 35 km/h, 35 km/h east, 12 s, 3.0 m down.

answer.html: 35 km/h is a scalar (magnitude only, a speed). 35 km/h east is a vector (magnitude and direction, a velocity). 12 s is a scalar (time). 3.0 m down is a vector (a displacement).

check.html: Adding a direction turns the speed into a velocity.

items.title: Lesson 2, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Draw a vector from one location to another in your school and explain how the drawing is a system model.

body.html: A sample: choose the gym door as origin with south as positive. Walking from the door to the trophy case 7 m south, then to the water fountain 11 m south, gives 𝛥𝑥<sub>1</sub> = + 7 m and 𝛥𝑥<sub>2</sub> = + 11 m.

answer.html: One arrow of length 18 m pointing south from the door to the fountain, labeled "displacement." Explanation: the person is modeled as a point, only the straight-line change in position is kept, and the arrow's length is proportional to 18 m.

check.html: The drawing keeps magnitude and direction, which is what a vector model needs.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 9: A mailbox is at 𝑥= 12 m and a tree is at 𝑥= 38 m on a number line with right positive. Describe the displacement from the tree to the mailbox.

body.html: Initial position (tree) 𝑥<sub>i</sub> = 38 m; final position (mailbox) 𝑥<sub>f</sub> = 12 m.
𝛥𝑥= 𝑥<sub>f</sub> −𝑥<sub>i</sub> = 12 m −38 m = −26 m.

answer.html: 26 m to the left (−26 m).

check.html: It is equal in size and opposite in direction to the displacement from the mailbox to the tree.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 10 Analyze: What is the sum of a vector 17 m south and a vector 6 m south?

body.html: Vectors in the same direction add by adding magnitudes.

answer.html: 23 m south

check.html: Same direction, so the resultant is larger than either vector.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 6: Choose a coordinate system for a boy riding a skateboard along a straight sidewalk that passes the front door of a house.

answer.html: One choice: put the origin at the spot on the sidewalk in front of the door, with the 𝑥-axis along the sidewalk and positive pointing in the direction he is rolling. Time starts at 𝑡= 0 when he passes the door. (Any origin on the line of his path with a stated positive direction works.)

check.html: A coordinate system needs a zero point and a positive direction, and both are given.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 7: A motion diagram shows 9 evenly spaced dots from Start to End. Draw a displacement vector for the object from the start to the end of the fifth time interval.

body.html: The fifth interval ends at the sixth dot (the first dot is the Start at time zero).
Draw an arrow from the first dot (Start) to the sixth dot.

answer.html: An arrow starting at the Start dot and ending at the sixth dot, pointing toward the End. Its length is five dot spacings.

check.html: Five intervals means five dot spacings.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 8: Two students each draw a position vector for a robot at 𝑡= 3 s, but the vectors point in opposite directions. Explain.

body.html: A position vector points from the origin to the object, so its direction depends on where each student put the origin.

answer.html: The students chose different origins (and/or positive directions). For example, if one origin is to the left of the robot and the other is to the right, the position vectors point opposite ways, even though the robot is in the same place.

check.html: Position depends on the coordinate system; displacement does not.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 9: A girl walks from home to the bus stop, and a motion diagram has 8 evenly spaced dots. Draw displacement vectors between each pair of dots.

body.html: 8 dots means 7 intervals; the dots are evenly spaced (she walks steadily).
Draw an arrow from each dot to the next, toward the Bus stop.

answer.html: Seven equal-length arrows, each from one dot to the next and pointing toward the Bus stop.

check.html: Equal spacing gives equal displacements.

items.title: Lesson 2 Focus Question: What are some different ways of describing and representing motion?

answer.html: Motion can be described with words, pictures, motion diagrams (with position and displacement vectors), data tables, position-time graphs, and equations, all using a coordinate system with an origin and a positive direction.

check.html: Matches the Study Guide for Lessons 2 and 3.

items.title: Lesson 2, Infer (Figure 7): What position would the arrow indicate if you chose the direction left of the origin as positive?

body.html: The sign of a position depends on the chosen positive direction. The point is 5 m to the left of the origin.

answer.html: +5 m (positive, since left is now the positive direction).

check.html: Reversing the positive direction flips the sign but not the magnitude.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: Explain how positive and negative positions are determined.

answer.html: First choose an origin and a positive direction. A position in the positive direction from the origin is positive; a position in the opposite direction is negative.

check.html: Consistent with Figure 7.

items.title: Lesson 2, Get It?: Describe the difference between a vector and a scalar.

answer.html: A vector has both magnitude and direction (such as position or displacement); a scalar has only magnitude (such as distance, time, or temperature).

check.html: "1.6 km" is a scalar; "1.6 km north" is a vector.

items.title: Lesson 2, Crosscutting Concepts (Systems and System Models): Vector drawing from one location to another.

body.html: A sample: choose the classroom door as origin with east as positive. Walking from the door to the teacher's desk 6 m east, then to the window 4 m east gives vectors 𝛥𝑥<sub>1</sub> = + 6 m and 𝛥𝑥<sub>2</sub> = + 4 m.

answer.html: One arrow of length 10 m pointing east from the door to the window, labeled "displacement." Explanation: the person is modeled as a point, only the straight-line position change is kept, and the length of the arrow is proportional to 10 m.

check.html: The drawing keeps magnitude and direction, which is what a vector model needs.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 9: Describe the displacement from the lamppost to the cactus.

body.html: Cactus at 𝑥= 5.0 m, lamppost at 𝑥= 25 m. Going from lamppost (initial) to cactus (final).
𝛥𝑥= 𝑥<sub>f</sub> −𝑥<sub>i</sub> = 5.0 m −25 m = −20 m.

answer.html: 20 m to the left (−20 m).

check.html: It is equal in size and opposite in direction to the displacement from cactus to lamppost.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 10 Analyze: What is the sum of a vector 12 m north and a vector 8 m north?

body.html: Vectors in the same direction add by adding magnitudes.

answer.html: 20 m north

check.html: Same direction, so the resultant is larger than either vector.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 6: Coordinate system for a girl swimming across a rectangular pool.

answer.html: One choice: put the origin at the corner/edge where she starts, with the 𝑥-axis along the line she swims (across the pool), positive pointing toward the far side. Time starts at 𝑡= 0 when she pushes off. (Any origin on the line of her path with a stated positive direction works.)

check.html: A coordinate system needs a zero point and a positive direction, and both are given.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 7: Draw a displacement vector for the car from the start to the end of the third time interval.

body.html: Dots (Start • • • • • • End) are evenly spaced; the third interval ends at the fourth dot.
Draw an arrow from the first dot (Start) to the fourth dot.

answer.html: An arrow starting at the Start dot and ending at the fourth dot, pointing toward the End. Its length is three dot spacings.

check.html: Three intervals means three dot spacings.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 8: Two students' position vectors for 𝑡= 2 s did not point in the same direction. Explain.

body.html: A position vector points from the origin to the object, so its direction depends on where each student put the origin and which direction they chose positive.

answer.html: The students chose different coordinate systems (different origins and/or positive directions). For example, if one origin is to the left of the object and the other to the right, the position vectors point opposite ways, even though the object is at the same place.

check.html: Position depends on the coordinate system; displacement does not.

items.title: Lesson 2 Check Your Progress, Problem 9: Displacement vectors between each pair of dots for the boy walking to school.

body.html: 10 dots from Home to School, evenly spaced (the boy walks steadily).
Draw an arrow from each dot to the next, toward School.

answer.html: Nine equal-length arrows, each from one dot to the next and pointing toward School.

check.html: Equal spacing gives equal displacements.
